# Copper February 2013 - Prices rallied strongly at the start of February, touching a new high for the year of just under $8350/t for 3-month copper on expectations of a sharp upturn in demand in China. However, momentum ran out of steam towards the end of the month on the realisation that it might be better to wait for an actual uptick in consumption before pushing prices too far. Meanwhile mixed signals from the US Fed added to the renewed caution, which resulted in copper losing some $400/t over the course of the third week of February until the market found technical support levels at the 200-day moving average of ~$7800/t. - Wood Mackenzie now estimates that world refined consumption was static in 2012 at 19.74M tonnes. Declining demand in Europe, Africa and Oceania offset modest growth in Asia, the Middle East, Latin America and North America. This month we focus on the major consuming markets of Japan, Germany and the United States. Only in the US are signs of brightness emerging with a good start to the year for the brass mill business. Activity in the construction and automotive industries is increasing which is benefiting downstream consumers, however aluminium is steadily taking share in the construction market with Encore Wire’s new aluminium building wire factory steadily expanding production. In Japan and Germany demand has begun the year slowly at lower levels than a year ago. German prospects depend greatly on a wider improvement in European demand while Japanese hopes are pinned on the potential benefits to the economy from a depreciating Yen. - Further long-term deals were concluded in February at the 2013 benchmark TCRC of $70/t & 7.0c/lb with OK Tedi and Anglo Chile understood to have settled with Japanese customers at this level. Negotiations are still believed to be ongoing between smelters and producers of ‘premium’ grade concentrates such as Highland Valley and Los Pelambres. The anticipated need for some large Chinese smelters to source significant amounts of material on the spot market later this year, following the declaration of holidays on long-term contracts with BHP Billiton, may have contributed to the downward pressure on Chinese buying terms during the month to levels last seen before the start of the annual benchmark negotiations i.e. to around $63/t and 6.3c/lb. #### **Copper key forecasts** ||**2012**|**%**|**2013**|**%**|**2014**|**%**|**2015**|**%**| |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| |**Global (kt)**||||||||| |Total Mine Production|16811|4.0|17622|4.8|19059|8.2|20044|5.2| |Total Smelter Production|15739|1.9|16595|5.4|17606|6.1|18426|4.7| |Refined Production|20258|2.7|21165|4.5|22479|6.2|23287|3.6| |Consumption|19744|0.0|20710|4.9|21756|5.1|22698|4.3| |Concentrate Market Balance|34||50||150||150|| |Metal Market Balance|513||456||722||589|| |MetalStocks- Days ofCons|67||72||81||87|| |**Prices**||||||||| |Cash

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market developments 

Prices rallied strongly at the start of February, touching a new high for the year of just under $8350/t for 3-month copper on expectations of a sharp upturn in demand in China.  However, momentum ran out of steam towards the end of the month on the realisation that it might be better to wait for an actual uptick in consumption before pushing prices too far. Meanwhile mixed signals from the US Fed added to the renewed caution. 

**Mood swings prices lower** In a similar vein to the start of 2012, market participants returned from Christmas holidays in optimistic mood and following what appeared to be a resolution to the US fiscal cliff, copper was driven higher at the beginning of this year and consolidated up around the $8000/t level.  At the start of February, renewed confidence in the global macro economic outlook drove cash quotes further upwards, towards the $8300/t.  A consensus appeared to have emerged that China had turned the corner and that following the Chinese New Year a strong uplift in demand was going to take place.  Against expectations, prices held their ground during this holiday period, before downbeat GDP data from European powerhouses Germany and France began to sour sentiment.  This signalled the beginning of an increasingly cautious tone to trading conditions.  At the same time the US Fed offered mixed signals over its strategy for the US economy.  Meanwhile, muted spot demand in China since that country’s return from the Lunar New Year break raised some concern about the strength of the expected upturn.  Ultimately, the combination of these factors resulted in copper losing some $400/t over the course of the third week of February in an uninterrupted decline until the market found technical support levels at the 200-day moving average of ~$7800/t. 

It was a measure of the confidence in the market through the first half of February that prices shrugged off this series of otherwise negative factors.  Firstly, exchange stocks continued to move higher in what has been an almost unbroken climb since November of last year, while the US dollar also strengthened against a number of currencies, which would normally be expected to place downward pressure on prices.  This begs the question whether fundamentals were asserting themselves then or are in fact reasserting themselves now.  From a fundamental perspective, the prevailing supply/demand balance should be a key determinant of the price and it is because of this that we anticipate an uplift in cash copper in the second quarter as Chinese demand improves.  We then expect prices to slide lower in the second half of the year as improving consumption is tempered by an expectation of stronger growth in copper supply.

The rise in material in exchange warehouses does at least mark a change from increases in invisible or at least semiinvisible stocks in Chinese bonded areas. We understand that bonded stocks are broadly unchanged since last month, although they may have edged marginally lower as a result of withdrawals prior to the Chinese New Year. As such, cathode in these warehouse zones stand at around 750kt at the end of February according to our estimates. Shanghai exchange inventories also dipped at the start of February, although in the first week back after the trading break this decline was immediately reversed, to end the month at 208kt. It was most likely that consumers elected to modestly restock ahead of the Lunar Holidays resulting in some withdrawals, but clearly it is too early to try to read anything meaningful into these movements. **Pace of Antwerp stock build slows** It has been one way traffic at LME warehouses for several months now, with total stocks having risen by almost 180kt since the end of November and as of 26th February they stand at 438kt. There have been Increases across the board, although the largest deliveries have been into North America and Europe. In Asia, stocks at South Korean locations have remained relatively stable over the past few months and indeed through February Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2013 Page 2 of 20 Copper Monthly Update but there has been a more significant increase in Malaysia and in Johor in particular. Here inventories are 62kt at the time of writing compared with 13kt at the end of November and 29kt at the end of January. The pace of cathodes moving on warrant has at least slowed in Europe, where a mountain of metal, and not just copper, has been built up over the past several months. Including the main LME metals of aluminium, lead, nickel and zinc, stocks in Antwerp currently stand at ~400kt, with copper accounting for around a quarter of this figure. At the end of September 2012 total stocks in Antwerp stood at 57kt, with no copper at all on warrant at that time. The reasons behind this build up have been discussed before but, in short, incentives have been offered in order to build a queue of metals such that warehouse owners can earn rent while only meeting minimum load out rates. This is particularly worthwhile in an uncertain demand outlook where it is not clear at what point metal may be required. **Does it really matter anyway?** The key question is whether the stock build in Antwerp really matters. There certainly has not been a major outcry from consumers that

copper is unavailable because of this, although it is also hard to get a handle on the transmission mechanism of higher premia because of the dearth of spot cathode business. As a result, it is hard to say what Rotterdam delivered premia are exactly, but we feel that levels of around $60/t are fairly representative. Tepid demand conditions in Europe have resulted in cathode being available if needed and it would take a strong upswing in demand to alter this scenario. Moreover, it is not clear what the driver would be for a significant upturn. As a result, semis producers seem relaxed for now about the potential for material being tied up, in part because their own customers further down the consumption chain have been extremely cautious in making bookings. Our feeling is that contract bookings at semis producers are similar to volumes last year but that increasing amounts of flexibility are being requested in those orders. In short, they are ordering material but only on the condition that they can then cancel if it is not needed and hence the overall tone in Europe is one of very guarded optimism. **Smaller but more frequent orders attract higher premia in US** In the US, premia edged higher this month to 5.756.25c/lb, although the increase was not reflective of improving demand conditions as such. Overall tonnages were described as reasonable but individual purchases were smaller and more frequent and as a result, attracted higher values. Similar to Europe, there is a sense of guarded optimism in the US, although the key difference between the two regions is that there are definite and encouraging signs of life in the North American construction market. #### **Copper spot premia – ($/t)** 180 10

The construction market in China is another story altogether and a renewed commitment from authorities to tackle house price inflation did nothing to improve the negative sentiment over the latter part of this month. The construction sector accounts for around 20% of Chinese copper consumption so is an important component of final demand, but, crucially, efforts to tame this sector tend to have knock on effects in other key sectors such as consumer durables, not to mention the impact on the broader economy and on market sentiment. Looking at Chinese demand as a whole, it is hard to get a true feel for the current picture due to the disruption from the Chinese Lunar holiday, however, one area that does appear to be doing very well is the HVACR market. Strength in this segment is leading to a solid uplift in production of air conditioner tube and this resulted in many tube mills closing for only a relativ

ely short period during the Chinese New Year break. This is also helping to drive demand for winding wire, although this is only serving to offset the sluggish performance of power cable and building wire production so far this year. In what was a relatively quiet month for spot cathode demand in China, premia ebbed lower to around $45-60/t at the end of February down from $60-65/t last month. It is likely that rising premia will be the first signal of the improving demand that we forecast during the second quarter of this year, unlike imports for which there is a lag in ordering and then a further delay until trade figures are reported. In any case the relevance of cathode imports as an indicator of Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2013 Page 3 of 20 Copper Monthly Update demand strength arguably is diminishing given the growth in domestic Chinese production of refined cathode following the expansion of smelting and refining capacity in the country over the past few years. These structural changes will therefore make the Chinese market less reliant upon imports of cathode and we forecast that net cathode imports into China will decline to ~2.5Mt in 2013 as imports fall and exports rise. In order to support the growth in refined production however, we also expect that imports of both copper concentrate and scrap will increase. We currently estimate concentrate imports will expand by around 15% and consumption of scrap at the smelters will grow by 6% to support our 370kt increase in refined production this year. #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 800 450

Another possible marker of improving demand would be a consistent decline in stocks, either on the Shanghai Exchange or in bonded warehouses, where, as mentioned they currently stand at around 750kt, although the degree to which these are accessible remains open to debate. The confusion relates to the extent to which this material is tied-up in financing deals and indeed, whether the same material has been used in multiple deals. An easing of credit conditions would likely have made such deals less attractive, but the government’s renewed commitment to clamping down on the luxury end of the property market does raise the spectre of this trade’s attractiveness either remaining ‘as is’ or increasing again. In these circumstances, a sharp rise in physical demand could result in prices running ahead of our forecast. Whilst we forecast that prices will be higher on average in the second quarter compared to the first, as we note above the illiquidity of bonded warehouses represents upside ri

sk to our forecast of $8200/t in Q2, coming off from our Q1 estimate of $8050/t. This will most likely mark the high point for the year as the increase in mine supply in the second half should bring pressure to bear on prices to result in cash quotes slipping to $8000/t in Q3 and moving lower still to $7500/t in the final three months of 2013. For 2013 as a whole the 4.5% increase in refined production supply will be outpaced by a 4.9% growth in demand to result in a surplus of ~450kt which is actually smaller than our latest estimate for 2012 of ~500kt. We forecast another year of strong growth in mine supply in 2014, which will push stocks higher still and result in prices moving even lower to $6950/t on average. ### **Japan** 

**Additional restructuring in the semis sector** Restructuring and consolidation at several Japanese semis manufacturers continues in light of increasing competition and a shrinking domestic market.  Several announcements were made over the last quarter of 2012 which were covered in detail in the November monthly.  Early in February 2013, Fujikura announced an early retirement programme whereby the company is looking to cut 300 staff across the group. The company also announced that it is to restructure its business into three units from four units currently and will now be split between energy & telecommunications (it is integrating its Metal Cable & Systems and Telecommunications units), electronics and finally automotive components.  Increasing competition due to a maturing and shrinking domestic telecommunications and power utility market and flood damage at its electronic business in Thailand were understood to be the main reasons for these changes.  The intention is to consolidate its business in Japan during 2013.  Fujikura Ltd intends to cut approximately 100 managerial staff, with a further 200 staff at domestic subsidiaries.  The program is expected to save the company an estimated Yen¥3.0Bn across the entire group.  The company will reinforce its automotive components business and plans to grow its overseas businesses in Europe and the USA.  The company also announced that it is revising its operating revenue lower by Yen¥1.0Bn (USD10.8M) to Yen¥7.0Bn (USD75.5M).  In addition to the restructuring of its copper wire rod and wire and cable business last year, Furukawa Electric Co. also announced the closure of its Tochigi-based Imaichi No.1 copper foil plant early this year.  The facility had been producing electrolytic copper foil for circuit boards in the electronics industry.  Lower profits and rising electricity prices were the reasons offered for the closure and production will be moved to Taiwan as it is more cost effective.  The Imaichi No.2 plant will also be shuttered by the end of September this year. 

**Auto production starts to take its toll on cable shipments** Japan's vehicle output rebounded by 18.4% in 2012 yearon-year to 9.943M units after a double-digit fall in 2011 according to the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association, with passenger car production growing the fastest at 19.5% year-on-year to 8.554M units, with truck output up 11.5% and bus production up 17.4% to 1.266M units and 122,220 units, respectively.  However in December alone, vehicle production posted a sharp 17.2% slump to 702,285 units and registered its fourth straight month of decline while exports declined 12.7% to 399,589 units. 

This downward trend was mirrored in Japan’s copper wire and cable shipments which fell for the second consecutive month in January, down by 2.7% year on year and 3.2% month on month, as demand from the automotive, electricmachin

ery and export industries all slowed. Shipments had peaked to 62.2kt in November 2012 but have subsequently fallen back over the past couple of months to a 7-month low of 54.5kt in January 2013. The impact of a weaker Yen has yet to be felt within the copper-cable sector with shipments for export slumping 28.2% to 1.1kt in January compared to levels a year earlier. Shipments to the automotive sector were 15.1% lower while deliveries to the electric-machinery industry declined 4.1% to 12.2kt according to data from the Japanese Electric Wire & Cable Makers Association. This decline is disappointing after the industry registered a year-on-year increase in total shipments of 1.9% in 2012 to 693.6kt up from 680.9kt in 2011. The Association expects that the recent declines in the Japanese currency, which has fallen more than 14% against the dollar over the past three months, will prompt a recovery in demand from the start of the new fiscal year in April. **Japanese cathode exports accelerate** As Japan’s domestic semis industry sector struggled, Japanese cathode producers lifted their exports in 2012 to 535kt, up 25.7% on year ago levels, with China, Taiwan, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand the main beneficiaries. Many Japanese manufacturers moved their production overseas after the Yen reached new highs in 2011, making their exports less competitive. In addition rising costs at home accelerated this year as power companies increased electricity charges to reflect higher energy imports after the Fukushima nuclear disaster. Japanese refined production rose by ~14% to 1.5Mt in 2012, compared to flat growth of ~1Mt in refined consumption and a ~2.8% decline in semis production. The segment which registered year-on year growth in production was wire rod in 2012, up by ~2.0%, supported by the 2% increase in wire and cable shipments during the year. **Copper tube imports rise** Japanese copper tube imports rose in 2012, up 3.1% with imports from Thailand up over 80% year on year. An unexpectedly hot summer in 2012 led to very high demand for air conditioners and tube supplies became increasingly tight throughout the supply chain. Additional imports were required to feed not only the acceleration in demand but also the replenishment of inventories that had been depleted across the supply chain. A portion of the Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2013 Page 6 of 20 Copper Monthly Update rise in imports included tube from Japanese companies which have relocated abroad. **Can Abe’s policies revive industry?** The recently elected Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe has vowed to pull the Japanese economy out of recession and end deflation with two key proposals; to print money and to spend money. While it remains to be seen if these policies will work longer term, sentiment surrounding Japan has changed with confidence already improving and money flowing back into the markets. In addition there has been a dramatic fall in the value of the Japanese Yen, which is positive for Japan's exporters. Indeed, exports rose in January for the first time in eight months as the Yen weakened. However, the cost of fuel imports has also increased sharply. Exports had been dented by several factors including the weak Eurozone and the territorial dispute with China. The latest data suggests this may be changing, with exports up 6.4%, driven mainly by shipments of manufactured goods. Japan's shipments to China rose for the first time since May 2012, up by 3% in January from levels a year ago, with exports to the USA up 10.9%, supporting hopes of further improvement. At the same time the pace of decline in exports to the European Union slowed during the month. The hope is that as shipments to key markets recover and the Yen continues to remain weak, Japan's export sector may see a sustained recovery and this will in turn lead to a boost in the manufacturing sector. In addition, the Government’s plan to boost spending on infrastructure should feed through to stronger shipments from the construction sector. Both factors should go some way to stimulating the copper semis industry during 2013. ### **United States** **Minor improvement in US consumption in 2012** Preliminary estimates indicate a modest 1.1% increase in US refined demand last year to 1.78M tonnes. Subject to the release of December data, copper wirerod production is believed to have risen by only 0.6% in 2012, a lower level than had been expected earlier in the year when growth prospects appeared stronger. Commercial production at SDI La Farga continues at low levels, awaiting further customer approvals before output is expanded to higher levels of capacity utilisation. AmRod has also suffered from disrupted production over the past few months. Production was halted for almost three weeks in November following flooding after Hurricane Sandy while output was also briefly suspended in early January this year due to a furnace problem which required a complete shutdown before restarting. In both instances the company made arrangements to meet customers’ requirements with minimal disruption to the market. **Construction ind

ustry output is rising…** The construction sector continues to show favourable signs of increased activity which should in time translate into higher copper demand.  January building permits rose 35% year-on-year to 925,000 units, while housing starts rose 24% year-on-year to 890,000 units.  There are signals that the higher level of activity is now starting to benefit consumers in a small way.  Although Encore Wire’s fourth quarter copper building wire volumes dropped 9.4% sequentially from the third quarter in the usual seasonal pattern volumes showed a mild 2.2% year-on-year increase compared to the fourth quarter of 2011.  This was, however, insufficient to prevent a 1.3% decline in the company’s copper building wire volumes for the whole year.  There are also more worrying indications that aluminium is continuing to capture market share from copper in the building wire market.  Aluminium products represented 5.1% of Encore Wire’s US dollar sales in the fourth quarter of 2012 versus a 3.6% share for the full year. This share is expected to expand more quickly in the future as the company’s new dedicated aluminium building wire factory became semi-operational in the fourth quarter of last year.  The US$40M 202,000 sq. ft. plant made its first

aluminium wire late last year and is currently receiving the last deliveries of equipment which will be installed during the first quarter.  The intention is that the plant will be fully operational by the second quarter of the year.  The company decided to expand into aluminium building wire to complement its existing copper building wire product range based on the large price spread and ratio relative to copper.  It also felt that it had to move with the marketplace as other manufacturers supplied both product lines.  In the past Encore Wire believed it had lost business because it had not been able to offer both product lines as part of the order to distributors whose contractor customers were requesting it. The company’s CFO Frank Bilban was quoted as saying, “It’s not our intention to push aluminium, but if you want it, we’ll have it.”  General Cable also said that its fourth quarter business was broadly ahead of expectations due to the gains in housing related utility and construction product shipments in the US. 

**…but the impact on the construction-related brass mill business will lag** The upturn should also be favourable for the brass mill business, though volumes have at best been stable recently compared to year-ago levels and after falling during the fourth quarter.  Commenting on the outlook for 2013, Greg Christopher CEO of Mueller Industries said, “Mueller’s business is significantly dependant on the housing and commercial construction industry.  After more than five years of decline and stagnation, the industry finally appears to be gaining positive momentum.  We look forward to the anticip

ated recovery with optimism.”  In the fourth quarter of 2012 total US production of copper tube fell 2.2% year-onyear to 55kt while output of brass rod, the other product line most driven by the construction market, dropped 7.1% yearon-year to 51kt. 

**Flat rolled brass mill product output strengthens in Q1** The fourth quarter of 2012 saw mixed but broadly favourable conditions in the flat rolled products business and this has continued into the opening quarter of 2013.  Copper plate, sheet and strip production fell 8.1% year-on-year to 25kt in the fourth quarter of last year while output of alloy plate, sheet and strip rose 7.1% to 56kt compared to the prior year period.  This trend of lower cost alloy sheet and strip demand gaining at the expense of more expensive pure copper products is a continuing facet of substitution due to high copper prices.  One of the fastest growing market segments is ammunition strip due to a surge in commercial sales of cartridges after the Sandy Hook elementary school shootings raised fears of tighter gun control legislation.  Walmart has imposed a sales limit of three boxes of ammunition per person per day due to limited supplies after sales surged as consumers stockpiled ammunition.  However there has also been an upturn in the interconnect, electronics, heat transfer and HVAC sectors so far in 2013, although coinage offtake has weakened.  Lead times at service centres extended past eight weeks in January for flat rolled products according to Aurubis Buffalo which is considering hiring more workers to meet the upsurge in demand. 

**Automotive sector keeps on moving** The automotive sector was a healthy source of demand in 2012 and this continued into 2013 with North American vehicle production growing 6.7% in January compared to prior year levels. Passenger car and medium/heavy truck assembly grew by 11-12% but light truck output increased by less than 3%. The expansion has supported demand for winding wire and connector terminals, though nearly all wiring harnesses are assembled and imported from abroad. 

### **Germany** 

**Sharp decline in refined consumption in 2012** German demand for refined copper is estimated to have fallen steeply by 9.1% to 1.14M tonnes in 2012 from 1.25M tonnes in 2011.  Although the domestic economy performed relatively well for the majority of the year a considerable proportion (~75%) of the country’s first use copper consumption (refined metal and direct use scrap) is actually dependant on demand from the rest of Europe and the rest of the world in the form of exports of copper and alloy semi-manufactures or insulated wire and cable.  If intermediate and final end use products were also included then the proportion would be even higher.  So the main problem for German semi-fabricators through 2012 and into 2013 has been the weakness of demand outside of Germany as domestic sales had held up well for most of the year. 

**Differing trends between wire rod and brass mill sectors**

Last year there were deeply contrasting trends between the rod and brass mill sectors. Wood Mackenzie estimate that total German rod production plummeted 13% to just under 650kt in 2012 from just over 740kt in 2011.  Exports of rod, drawn wire and stranded conductors fell by more than 50kt to around 340kt from over 390kt in the prior year.  Not only was demand softer but German mills also suffered the loss of some market share due to the more flexible terms offered by competing European mills to preserve their volumes at the expense of their margins.  This also affected German rod sales in the domestic market as imports of rod, drawn wire and stranded conductors fell only 6% capturing some market share from local German mills.  By contrast, the brass mill and castings sector only saw around a 5% decline in semis output from 806kt in 2011 to 770kt in 2012 according to Wood Mackenzie estimates.  Domestic demand held up better than was the case in wire rod and exports were only moderately impacted in the high volume copper and copper alloy plate, sheet and strip and the alloy rod and bar product lines. Strong demand from the automotive sector supported sheet and strip demand for terminals and connectors through the first three quarters of 2012 but offtake weakened in the fourth quarter.  German auto sales began 2013 showing some signs of weakness against the healthy levels of 2012 with January passenger car registrations down almost 9% to 192,000 units, suggesting a much tougher year ahead. 

**Aurubis sees declining semis production** Leading European copper producer Aurubis reported a further fall in its semis production in the October to December quarter, although cathode production rose slightly to 234kt in the three month period, compared to 232kt in the prior year.   Rod production in the quarter dropped 19% year-on-year to 127kt

versus 156kt in the same quarter of 2011.  For the calendar year of 2012, which differs to the company’s fiscal year, Aurubis’ rod production dropped by 17% to 617kt against output of 743kt in calendar year 2011.  The company attributed the most recent quarter’s decline to weak demand from Southern Europe and destocking by consumers ahead of the year end. (CNMC), was initially ordered to close by the Zambia Environmental Management Agency (ZEMA) following allegations of excessive sulphur dioxide emissions. ## Production news 

**Annual output from Chile rises despite operational problems** According to statistics from the Chilean Copper Commission (COCHILCO), the country’s copper mine production for 2012 was 5.43Mt, a 3% rise on the equivalent figure for 2012.  The increase was achieved despite the fact that output from some major mines was significantly lower than in 2011.  A variety of reasons including low grades, adverse weather, safety stoppages and technical problems saw production at Collahuasi limited to 282kt compared to 453kt during 2011.  Combined commercial production reported by Codelco for its Chuquicamata and Radomiro Tomic operations was 784kt compared to 914kt in 2011 as output was impacted by lower grades and unscheduled smelter outages.  Declines at these mines were mitigated by increases in output elsewhere.  Escondida benefited in the second half of the year from increased head grades and the successful completion of large scale maintenance programs, reaching an annual total of 1.08Mt compared to 818kt during 2011. Although below initial forecasts due to lower than expected head grades and poor recovery, production at Los Bronces reached 365kt in 2012 (+65%) as the $2.8Bn mill expansion headed towards design throughput levels.  Elsewhere, 2012 output reported by Antofagasta Minerals for its new Esperanza mine was 173kt compared to 97kt during 2011. 

**Production also up in Peru** Statistics from the Peruvian Ministry of Energy and Mines showed the country’s mined copper production rose to 1.30Mt in the 2012, a 5.1% increase on 2011.  The principal contributor to this increase was the Antamina mine where the commissioning of a $1.3bn project to increase mill throughput from 95kt/d to 130kt/d enabled production to reach 447kt compared to 334kt in 2011.  Combined production from Southern Copper’s Toquepala and Cuajone operations reached 311kt compared to 295kt in 2011 due to improved head grades.  Increases in output at these operations were partially offset by lower production elsewhere.  Copper produced at Cerro Verde was 279kt, down by 8% on 2011 levels due to anticipated lower head grades.  Meanwhile, output at Xstrata’s Tintaya operation which has been replaced by Antapaccay totalled 46kt during 2012 compared to 95kt the previous year. 

**Southern Copper labour settlement** Southern Copper is reported to have reached agreement with unionised workers at its Cuajone and Toquepala mines and Ilo smelter.  The bulk of these members at the Peruvian operations have been awarded a 6.5% rise for 2013 and 5% each for the subsequent two years. 

**Padcal to re-open temporarily** Reports from the Philippines suggest that the government may

allow Philex Mining Corporation to temporarily reopen its Padcal mine.  Under the plans the mine would be allowed to operate under supervision for four months in order to generate material that will be used to strengthen the tailings dam.  Production from the mine was suspended in August after tailings spillages that followed heavy rainfall.  At full capacity the mine produces 20kt/a of copper in concentrate for export primarily to Japanese smelters.

**Boleo reach funding deal, but project timing remains uncertain** Baja Mining Corporation has announced that a consortium of Korean companies headed by Korea Resources Corporation (KORES) has agreed to conclude the $443M additional investment required to complete the construction of the Boleo project in Mexico.  The project, which is forecast to produce up to 55kt/a of SxEw cathode plus 2.2kt/a of cobalt cathode and 45kt/a of zinc sulphate, was originally budgeted to require a capital investment of $1.4Bn.  Construction was put on hold in mid-2012 following cost over runs. The Korean consortium, which has already advanced $259M of the extra $443M required to complete the project, has now agreed to contribute the balance in three stages, although the schedule for this remains unconfirmed.  Upon completion of the payments the Korean consortium would gain a 90% interest in the project with Baja Mining Corporation retaining the remaining 10%.  Earlier in the month, Baja Mining announced that work on a NI 43-101 compliant technical report on the project was ongoing, but that a publication date could not be confirmed. 

**Glencore expansion in DRC** Total copper production reported by Glencore from own feed sources at its African operations amounted to 279kt during 2012, a 9% increase on 2011.  The rise was principally due to increased output of copper cathode from the Mutanda operation in the DRC in which Glencore holds a 60% stake and where overall production amounted to 87kt during 2012, of which 83.5kt was in the form of SxEw.  Cathode production capacity at the Mutanda operation is now reported to be 110kt/a

.  A feasibility study for a milling operation rated to produce an additional 110kt/a of copper in concentrate at Mutanda is scheduled for completion during Q1 2013.  Glencore also holds a 37.5% interest in the neighbouring Kansuki deposit where it reported $413M out if a $507M investment in a mine and plant development had been completed by the end of 2012.  The combined production capacity of Kansuki and Mutanda is targeted to be 200kt/a by the end of 2013.  Production at Katanga Mining in which Glencore holds a 75.2% was adversely impacted by interruptions to its power supply during 2012 resulting in 67 days of lost production.  Combined output of copper in concentrate and copper metal from the Luilu metallurgical plant was 93kt, a 2% rise on 2011.  Initial production from a pre-existing electro-refinery converted to operate as an SxEw plant was reported in December with this facility understood to be rated to produce 120kt/a of copper cathode.  Commissioning of a new power converter as part of a World Bank power project and a new synchronous condenser under Katanga’s agreement with local utility company SNEL also took place towards the end of 2012.   Glencore is also taking steps to secure the power supply for all its operations in the DRC by entering into a partnership with SNEL and contractor EGMF to refurbish two turbines at the Inga hydroelectric dam which could potentially supply 450MW by the end of 2015. 

**Lumwana plans revised** Barrick reported that 2012 production from its Lumwana operation in Zambia amounted to 179Mlb (81kt).  The company also announced that following an exploration and in-fill drilling program the life-of-mine plan for the operation had been revised to reflect revised operating costs with the result that a $3.0Bn impairment charge had been incurred and expansion plans at the site had been put on hold. 

**Environmental approval for Tampakan, but hurdles remain** Sagittarius Mines Inc. (SMI), developers of the Tampakan copper and gold mine has announced that it has received an environmental compliance certificate from the Philippines Department of Environment and Natural Resources. The project is located in the South Cotabato province of the country, where a local ordinance banning open pit mining was passed in 2010.   Despite pressure from the national government local officials have indicated that they intend to uphold the ban until it is ‘declared unconstitutional by a competent court’.  Local elections in the province of South Cotabato are scheduled for May of this year.  Any further progress in the approval process for Tampakan is unlikely until the identity of the new Governor and political make-up of the provincial legislature are confirmed.  SMI is owned by Xstrata (62.5%) and Indophil Resources (37.5%).  In 2010 the pre-production capital cost of the project, which is forecast to average 380kt/a of copper in concentrate production over its first 10 years or operation, was estimated at $5.1Bn.
